text:
When the major’s wife has come this far, she always looks up, gazes about her, sees the closed door, and knows where she is.

Then she wonders whether she is going mad, and sits down to think and rest. But after a while she is at it again, adding ells and fathoms into half-miles and miles, taking short rests in the Finnish huts, and sleeping neither night nor day until she has once more covered the twenty miles.

During all the time she has been held prisoner, she has hardly ever slept.

And the two women who have come to look after her watch her with anguish.

The young countess would always remember her afterward as she walked there then. She often sees her afterward in her dreams, and then awakens from the vision with her eyes wet with tears and a lament on her lips.

The old woman has deteriorated distressingly; her hair looks thin, and loose tangles protrude from the narrow braid. Her face is slack and sunken, her clothes disordered and torn. But despite all this she retains so much of the exalted ruler who commanded everyone that she inspires not only pity but also reverence.

But what the countess clearly remembered was the eyes, sunken, turned inward, not yet deprived of all the light of reason, but almost ready to go out, with a spark of wildness lurking in their depths, so that one could not help dreading and fearing that in the next moment the old woman would be upon one, her teeth ready to bite, her fingers to claw.

They have now stood there for quite some time when the major’s wife suddenly stops before the young woman and looks at her sternly. The countess takes a step backward and grasps Mrs. Scharling’s arm.

The features of the major’s wife suddenly take on life and expression; her eyes look out upon the world with full understanding.

“Oh no, oh no,” she says with a little smile, “it is not quite so bad as that, my dear young lady.”

She now invites them to sit down and also seats herself. She assumes an air of old-fashioned stateliness, familiar from the great feasts at Ekeby and the royal balls at the governor’s residence in Karlstad. They forget the rags and the prison and see only the proudest and richest lady in Värmland.

“My dear countess!” she says. “What could induce you to leave the dance to seek out a lonely old woman like me? You must be very kind.”

Countess Elisabet cannot answer. Her voice is choked with emotion. Mrs. Scharling answers in her stead that she has been unable to dance because she has been thinking of the major’s wife.

“Dear Mrs. Scharling,” the major’s wife replies, “have things now come to such a pass with me that I disturb the young in their joy? You must not weep over me, my dear young countess,” she continued. “I am a wicked old woman who deserves my fate. You do not consider it right to strike one’s mother, do you?”

“No, but—”

The major’s wife interrupts her and brushes the curly, fair hair back from her forehead.

“Child, child,” she says, “how could you go and marry that foolish Henrik Dohna?”

“But I love him.”

“I see how it is, I see how it is,” says the major’s wife. “A good child and nothing more, weeping with the sorrowful and laughing with the merry. And compelled to say ‘yes’ to the first man who says, ‘I love you.’ Yes, certainly, yes. Go in and dance now, my dear young countess! Dance and be glad! There is nothing evil in you.”

“But I wanted to do something for the major’s wife.”

“Child,” says the major’s wife solemnly, “there once lived an old woman at Ekeby who held the winds of heaven captive. Now she is imprisoned, and the winds are free. Is it strange that a storm is sweeping through the land?

I, who am old, have seen it before, countess. I know it. I know that the thundering storm of God is coming upon us. Now it rushes over the great realms, now over the small, forgotten communities. God’s storm forgets no one. It comes upon great and small alike. It is glorious to see God’s storm coming.

Storm of God, you blessed tempest of the Lord, blow over the earth! Voices in the air, voices in the waters, resound and strike terror! Make God’s storm thunder! Make God’s storm terrifying! May the gusts sweep out across the land, hurl themselves against tottering walls, break the locks that have rusted and the houses that lean toward their fall!

Anguish shall spread across the land. The little birds’ nests shall fall from their hold upon the branch. The hawk’s nest at the top of the pine shall be shaken to the ground with a great crash, and even into the owl’s nest in the mountain cleft the wind shall hiss with its dragon tongue.

We thought that all was well here among us, but it was not so. God’s storm is surely needed. I understand that, and I do not complain. I only wish that I might go to my mother.”

She suddenly collapses.

“Go now, young woman!” she says. “I have no more time. I must go. Go now, and beware of those who ride upon the storm clouds!”

With that she resumes her pacing. Her features go slack, her gaze turns inward. The countess and Mrs. Scharling must leave her.

As soon as they are back among the dancers, the young countess goes straight up to Gösta Berling.

“I am to give Mr. Berling the major’s wife’s greetings,” she says. “She expects Mr. Berling to get her out of prison.”

“Then she will have to wait, countess.”

“Oh, help her, Mr. Berling!”

Gösta stares darkly before him. “No,” he says, “why should I help her? What gratitude do I owe her? Everything she has done for me has been to my ruin.”

“But, Mr. Berling—”

“If she had not existed,” he says vehemently, “I would now be sleeping up there beneath the eternal forests. Am I obliged to risk my life for her because she made me a cavalier at Ekeby? Does the countess think that much renown comes with that office?”

The young countess turns away from him without answering. She is angry.

She goes to her place, thinking bitter thoughts about the cavaliers. They have come here with French horns and fiddles and intend to let the bows scrape across the strings until the horsehair has worn away, without thinking that the merry notes carry into the prisoner’s wretched room. They come here to dance until the soles of their shoes turn to dust, and do not think that their old benefactress may see their shadows swing past inside the misted panes. Ah, how gray and ugly the world had become! Ah, what a shadow distress and hardness cast over the young countess’s soul!
